In [[mathematics]], and more specifically in [[polyhedral combinatorics]], a '''Goldberg polyhedron''' is a [[convex polyhedron]] made from [[hexagon]]s and [[pentagon]]s. They were first described in 1937 by [[Michael Goldberg (mathematician)|Michael Goldberg]] (1902–1990). They are defined by three properties: each [[Face (geometry)|face]] is either a pentagon or hexagon, exactly three faces meet at each [[Vertex (geometry)|vertex]], and they have [[rotational icosahedral symmetry]]. They are not necessarily [[Reflection symmetry|mirror-symmetric]]; e.g. {{math|GP(5,3)}} and {{math|GP(3,5)}} are [[enantiomorph]]s of each other.  A Goldberg polyhedron is a [[dual polyhedron]] of a [[geodesic polyhedron]].

A consequence of [[Euler's polyhedron formula]] is that a Goldberg polyhedron always has exactly 12 pentagonal faces. Icosahedral symmetry ensures that the pentagons are always [[regular polygon|regular]] and that there are always 12 of them. If the vertices are not constrained to a sphere, the polyhedron can be constructed with planar equilateral (but not in general equiangular) faces.

Simple examples of Goldberg polyhedra include the [[dodecahedron]] and [[truncated icosahedron]]. Other forms can be described by taking a [[chess]] [[Knight (chess)|knight]] move from one pentagon to the next: first take {{mvar|m}} steps in one direction, then turn 60° to the left and take {{mvar|n}} steps. Such a polyhedron is denoted {{math|GP(''m'',''n'')}}. A dodecahedron is {{math|GP(1,0)}}, and a [[truncated icosahedron]] is {{math|GP(1,1)}}.

A similar technique can be applied to construct polyhedra with [[tetrahedral symmetry]] and [[octahedral symmetry]]. These polyhedra will have triangles or squares rather than pentagons. These variations are given Roman numeral subscripts denoting the number of sides on the non-hexagon faces: {{math|GP{{sub|III}}(''n'',''m'')}}, {{math|GP{{sub|IV}}(''n'',''m'')}}, and {{math|GP{{sub|V}}(''n'',''m'')}}.

== Elements ==
The number of vertices, edges, and faces of {{math|GP(''m'',''n'')}} can be computed from {{mvar|m}} and {{mvar|n}}, with 
<math display=block>
 T = m^2 + mn + n^2 = (m + n)^2 - mn,
</math>
depending on one of three symmetry systems:<ref>Clinton’s Equal Central Angle Conjecture, JOSEPH D. CLINTON</ref> 
The number of non-hexagonal faces can be determined using the Euler characteristic, as demonstrated [[Euler characteristic#Soccer_ball|here]].

== Construction ==
Most Goldberg polyhedra can be constructed using [[Conway polyhedron notation]] starting with (T)etrahedron, (C)ube, and (D)odecahedron seeds. The [[Chamfer (geometry)|chamfer]] operator, {{mvar|c}}, replaces all edges by hexagons, transforming {{math|GP(''m'',''n'')}} to {{math|GP(2''m'',2''n'')}}, with a {{mvar|T}} multiplier of 4. The ''truncated kis'' operator, {{math|1=''y'' = ''tk''}}, generates {{math|GP(3,0)}}, transforming {{math|GP(''m'',''n'')}} to {{math|GP(3''m'',3''n'')}}, with a {{mvar|T}} multiplier of 9.

For class 2 forms, the ''dual kis'' operator, {{math|1=''z'' = ''dk''}}, transforms {{math|GP(''a'',0)}} into {{math|GP(''a'',''a'')}}, with a {{mvar|T}} multiplier of 3. For class 3 forms, the ''whirl'' operator, {{mvar|w}}, generates {{math|GP(2,1)}}, with a {{mvar|T}} multiplier of 7. A clockwise and counterclockwise whirl generator, {{math|1=''w''{{overline|''w''}} = ''wrw''}} generates {{math|GP(7,0)}} in class 1. In general, a whirl can transform a {{math|GP(''a'',''b'')}} into {{math|GP(''a'' + 3''b'', 2''ab'')}} for {{math|''a'' > ''b''}} and the same chiral direction. If chiral directions are reversed, {{math|GP(''a'', ''b'')}} becomes {{math|GP(2''a'' + 3''b'', ''a'' − 2''b'')}} if {{math|''a'' ≥ 2''b''}}, and {{math|GP(3''a'' + ''b'', 2''b'' − ''a'')}} if {{math|''a'' < 2''b''}}.
